subtitle: Balance models, the properties of equality, and why one move flips an inequality sign

problems.desc: Part (a): a correct response says 7 was added to both sides -- the addition property of equality. Full credit states the operation and that it was done to both sides; naming only the number 7 does not.

Part (b): a correct response says both sides were divided by 3 -- the division property of equality, equivalently multiplying both sides by one third. Full credit states the operation and that both sides received it.

Part (a): a correct response names the two moves in order -- 2x was subtracted from both sides (subtraction property of equality), then 1 was added to both sides (addition property). Full credit names both moves and says each was applied to both sides; saying only that the work is right does not.

Part (b): a correct response says the sign does change, and that it changes at the step where both sides are divided by -2. Dividing by a negative reverses the order of the two sides, so greater-than-or-equal becomes less-than-or-equal. Full credit identifies that step as the reason; answering yes or no with no step named earns half credit.

Part (a): a correct response says the first step is the illegal one: 3(x+2) was rewritten as 3x+2, so the factor 3 reached only the x and not the 2. It should be 3x+6. This is not a property of equality at all -- nothing was done to both sides -- it is a mis-application of the distributive property to one side. Full credit points at that first line.

Part (b): a correct response justifies each move in turn -- multiplying both sides by 3 to clear the fraction (multiplication property of equality), distributing on the left is a rewrite of one side only (distributive property, not a property of equality), then subtracting 2x and subtracting 12 from both sides (subtraction property), and finally dividing both sides by 1 or reading the value off. Full credit distinguishes the moves done to BOTH sides from the rewrite done to ONE side.
